content: Potassium manganate is a chemical compound with the molecular formula K₂MnO₄. This compound appears as a green salt and serves as an intermediate in the industrial production of potassium permanganate, a widely used chemical. Despite occasional confusion between potassium manganate and potassium permanganate, they are distinct compounds with significantly different chemical properties. The structure of potassium manganate consists of potassium cations (K⁺) and manganate anions (MnO₄²⁻). The Mn-O bond lengths in K₂MnO₄ are approximately 1.66 Å, which is slightly longer than the Mn-O bond lengths observed in potassium permanganate (KMnO₄). In industrial settings, potassium manganate is synthesized by treating manganese dioxide (MnO₂) with air in the presence of potassium hydroxide (KOH). This process produces a green-colored melt, which is indicative of the formation of potassium manganate. A simple test for the presence of manganese in an unknown sample involves heating the sample in strong KOH under air. The appearance of a green coloration confirms the presence of manganese, as this color arises from an intense absorption at 610 nm. In laboratory conditions, potassium manganate can be prepared by heating a solution of potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) in concentrated KOH, followed by cooling to yield green crystals. This reaction highlights the relatively rare role of hydroxide ions as reducing agents. Additionally, solutions of K₂MnO₄ can be generated by stirring a solution of KMnO₄ in 5–10 M KOH at room temperature for a day, followed by the removal of insoluble manganese dioxide (MnO₂). The concentration of K₂MnO₄ in such solutions can be determined by measuring their absorbance at 610 nm. The one-electron reduction of permanganate (MnO₄⁻) to manganate (MnO₄²⁻) can also be achieved using iodide ions as the reducing agent. This reaction is visually marked by a color change from the purple of permanganate to the green of manganate. This process demonstrates that manganate(VII) can act as an electron acceptor in addition to its usual role as an oxygen-transfer reagent. Barium manganate (BaMnO₄) can be synthesized by reducing KMnO₄ with iodide in the presence of barium chloride (BaCl₂). Similar to barium sulfate (BaSO₄), barium manganate exhibits very low solubility in nearly all solvents. At lower pH levels, the manganate ion (MnO₄²⁻) undergoes disproportionation to form permanganate ions (MnO₄⁻) and manganese dioxide (MnO₂). The vivid color changes associated with this reaction have led to the manganate/manganate(VII) pair being referred to as a chemical chameleon. This disproportionation reaction, which becomes rapid at concentrations below 1 M, follows bimolecular kinetics.
